item.title: Modeling the Joint Distribution of Box Score Statistics: A Gaussian Copula Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.10152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What is the probability that LeBron James records at least 27 points, 7 rebounds, and 7 assists tonight? While an interesting statistical question by itself, the rise of sports betting and multi-leg parlays has made answering this question increasingly relevant. However, coming up with an estimated likelihood is tricky, since box score statistics aren't independent. We estimate the joint probability that a player reaches a combination of thresholds in points, assists, and rebounds using a Gaussian copula, fit separately for each player using only their previous games. We compare it with two benchmarks: the product of the empirical marginal probabilities (i.e. assuming independence) and the empirical frequency of the joint event. Across ~22,000 player-observations, the Gaussian copula performs on par or better than either benchmark at lower threshold levels, with large gains at high joint exceedance levels. Because it is generative, the model also allows for probabilistic calculations for combinations that a player has rarely or never produced.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Watts

item.title: An Exploratory Pilot Analysis of Paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 SPR Sensorgrams: Retained Response, Early Shape, and Complementarity
item.description: arXiv:2611.10306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We conduct a retrospective exploratory pilot analysis of paired PD-L1 and Siglec-15 surface plasmon resonance (SPR) trajectories, examining retained response, dual-marker fusion, and additional early-shape information. Numerical matching links the original exports to previously quality-selected data: 69 files represent 68 distinct source column pairs from 10 cancer and 10 healthy study patients. Existing exclusions and truncations are preserved. All 20 patients contribute to development and exploration; no independent validation cohort is available. Because historical per-scan manual alignment offsets are unavailable, the numerical comparisons are conditional on separately documented candidate response-transition intervals rather than verified injection-event times. Patient-level paired comparisons, leave-pair-out internal assessment, empirical false-positive budgets, and timing sensitivity are implemented in reproducible Python code. Under candidate alignment, the dual-marker retained-response sum has an apparent AUC of 0.570, with a fixed-score bootstrap 95% interval of [0.300, 0.820]. In the nested 13-patient shape subset, retention alone and the fixed 85:15 retention-shape score both have AUC 0.619; the small paired increment changes direction across the -1,0,+1 minute shift scenarios. At a same-sample budget of two false positives among ten controls, dual-marker retention identifies four cancer cases, compared with two for PD-L1 and three for Siglec-15. Analytical bounds describe feature stability under stated measurement assumptions but do not identify the cause of weak discrimination. The study provides a traceable analysis framework and operating-point hypotheses for independent evaluation; the small development cohort does not establish diagnostic utility or a reliable fusion or shape advantage.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Wang (Mathematics,Mathematics Education, National Institute of Education, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore)

item.title: Measuring Public Institutions and their Agents: Disparities and Agreement, with Application to Asylum Decisions in the U.S. Immigration Courts
item.description: arXiv:2611.10308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public institutions derive their legitimacy from the professionalism and impartiality of their agents. In order to maintain standards of conduct, the performance of an agent is often compared to the performance of her peers. But public institutions typically assign agents to different tasks, and as a result, naive comparisons may reflect the difficulty of the assignment and not an agent's performance. To address this concern, we develop measures of disparity and agreement that compare an agent's performance with the potential performance of randomly selected peers who could have been assigned the same set of tasks. We then give realistic conditions under which disparity is identified from the marginal distribution of each agent's actions. We also show how agreement, which is generally unidentified when agents are assigned to different tasks, can be bounded or estimated under sensitivity assumptions about the dependence between potential outcomes. Finally, we use a nonparametric Bayesian model to examine applications for asylum filed between 2007 and 2014 in the widely studied and often maligned U.S. immigration courts. Our results do not support the picture of widespread partiality asserted in previous empirical work. At both the judge and court level, we find limited disparity and substantial potential agreement.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Auerbach, Michael E. Sobel

item.title: Regularity in Cryptocurrency Market Cycles: A Halving-to-Halving Analysis Using Data from Google Trends and Wikipedia
item.description: arXiv:2611.10674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bitcoin halvings provide a natural temporal structure for studying long-term dynamics of cryptocurrency markets. This paper presents a methodological framework for analyzing the regularity of Bitcoin and aggregate cryptocurrency market cycles by normalizing historical periods between consecutive halving events and projecting them onto a common relative-time scale expressed as the percentage of cycle completion. The proposed framework integrates market variables, namely Bitcoin price and aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, with measures of public attention derived from Google Trends search volume and Wikipedia pageviews. To obtain long-horizon daily attention indices, Google Trends data are reconstructed from overlapping 90-day windows linked by median scale ratios, following established approaches to combining high-frequency Google Trends samples. Rather than attempting to forecast future prices, the study aims to compare historical cycles, identify recurring temporal patterns, and evaluate the relationship between market dynamics and retail investor interest across different cycle-relative stages. Exploratory results point to a possible recurring structure. The maxima of the aggregate market capitalization in the two most recent completed cycles occurred at 39.0% and 37.9% of cycle completion, and the highest value of the ongoing cycle observed to date at 38.1% (534-547 days after the respective halvings), although the corresponding multiple of the halving-day value fell from 66 to 1.8. Public attention shows a similar compression of peak multiples, but not a similar timing. The paper also discusses current data limitations and outlines future research directions, including formal lead-lag analyses and expanded multi-asset investigations.
item.dc:creator: Marek Zatwarnicki, Piotr Stolarski, W{\l}odzimierz Lewoniewski

item.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species
item.description: arXiv:2611.10871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Halder, Joseph R. Stinziano, Joshua Persi

item.title: Digital Twins for Clinical Development: A Five-Level Framework from Prognostic Adjustment to In-Silico Trials
item.description: arXiv:2611.10888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly discussed in drug development, often narrowly as virtual control arms or synthetic data. We propose a broader framework for data-driven clinical digital twins, organized into five levels according to how much of the trial data matrix of baseline covariates, treatment, and responses is generated by a statistical or machine-learning model trained on historical, external, or real-world data. The levels are: (1) prognostic score adjustment, (2) response trajectory prediction, (3) virtual control, (4) synthetic population, and (5) fully synthetic patients and responses. For each level we describe the estimation workflow, the development decision it can support, and the principal statistical guardrail. As the share of model-generated information increases, the inferential weight placed on the model grows and regulatory maturity generally declines. We argue that credibility requirements should therefore scale with context of use, characterized jointly by model influence and decision consequence, following a risk-based credibility framework. We identify four recurring credibility questions (drift and transportability, estimand alignment, compounding error, and data quality and provenance), summarize the current regulator landscape, and discuss bottlenecks in data, model transferability, collaboration, and lifecycle governance. The central message for statisticians is to start from the decision rather than the model, and to earn trust use by use.
item.dc:creator: Jingyuan Yang

item.title: Zero Replacement and Latent Profiles in Short Media Diaries: Checking Recording Status Before User Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short media diaries contain many zeros because many activities go unrecorded during the observation period. Log-ratio analysis of time allocation requires these zeros to be replaced with small positive values; as a result, all respondents who did not record an activity receive nearly the same value. We examined how such zero replacement affects classification in latent profile analysis and propose checks to perform before profiles are interpreted. Three-day diaries of 8,089 adults from the 2025 Korea Media Panel Survey were converted into nine-part time-use compositions. Gaming was not recorded by 88.9% of the respondents, and in every model with two to eight profiles and a covariance matrix held equal across profiles, respondents who recorded gaming and those who did not were classified into different profiles. Even when the replacement value equaled the minimum recording unit (5 min/day), the two-profile classification largely matched gaming recording status, and the two groups separated more sharply as the replacement value decreased, until the separation was complete. Before naming profiles, researchers should therefore check the proportion of respondents who did not record each activity and its replacement value, the same proportion within each profile, and the distribution of usage time among those who recorded the activity.
item.dc:creator: Eunjeong Song, Sehee Hong

item.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.
item.dc:creator: Andrew R Weckstein, Issa J Dahabreh, Marinka Zitnik, Sonia Hern\'andez-D\'iaz, Sebastian Schneeweiss

item.title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle
item.description: arXiv:2611.11743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measurement systems generate uncertain information that downstream manufacturing decisions often consume as if fixed. This structured integrative review examines how measurement error, uncertainty, GR\&R estimates, calibration evidence, and drift information are handed off into capability inference, retrospective Phase I reference estimation, prospective Phase II monitoring, operational action, and requalification. Studies are compared by the upstream uncertain object, whether it is known, calibrated, or estimated, its propagation mechanism, the downstream decision, and the validation boundary. The synthesis distinguishes recorded production data from latent-process targets: measurement-system information calibrates limits, uncertainty statements, replication, guard bands, or losses, but does not reveal the realized random error in an individual record. Within the retained literature, measurement-to-capability and measurement-to-monitoring mechanisms are more extensively represented by model-based studies, whereas prospective evidence is thinner where statistical results must support source attribution, cost-sensitive action, and requalification. A decision-handoff spine separates measurement generation, statistical inference, and operational validation so that capability, stability, attribution, and intervention effectiveness are not conflated. The review is integrative rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is an auditable measurement-science framework that preserves provenance, information status, validity conditions, and downstream use while identifying claims that are model-supported, conditionally calibrated, or not yet operationally validated.
item.dc:creator: Fei Jiang, Lei Yang

item.title: Short-term associations between wild-bird and mammalian high pathogenic avian influenza detection in the United States
item.description: arXiv:2611.12005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) detections in mammals have raised concern about repeated wildlife spillover and the targeting of mammalian surveillance. We evaluated whether wild-bird detection records contained short-term explanatory and predictive information about mammalian detections in the United States. Public surveillance records from April 2022 to July 2026 comprised 18,523 wild-bird and 815 mammalian detections. Monthly state-level mammalian counts were analysed using negative-binomial mixed models adjusted for seasonality, preceding mammalian detections and state-level heterogeneity. The selected model contained contemporaneous and one-month-lagged same-state wild-bird counts. A doubling of one plus the contemporaneous wild-bird count was associated with a 57.9% increase in the expected mammalian count (95% CI 43.5-73.8%), and a doubling of the preceding-month count with a 15.9% increase (5.2-27.8%). Bordering-state exposure did not improve fit. In a six-month temporal holdout, adding same-state wild-bird exposure reduced mean absolute error by 23.8% and root mean squared error by 27.9%, although total detections remained overpredicted. After exact-row deduplication, the corresponding effects were 59.7% and 13.3%. Wild-bird surveillance records contained short-term, geographically local information about mammalian HPAI detection activity, but the associations do not establish direct transmission and require further calibration before operational forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Hammed Olawale Fatoyinbo

item.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
item.description: arXiv:2611.12193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.
item.dc:creator: Henning Bonart

item.title: The Fragility Of Synthetic Populations Over Time: An Evaluation Of Forecasting Strategies For Agent-Based Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.12344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent-based simulation models are widely used to assess the future mobility projects. However, their effectiveness hinges on the accuracy of synthetic populations, which are often generated using data from a single reference year. This study explores the temporal validity of these populations by evaluating their performance over multi-year datasets in a simulation-like environment. We focus on multi-dimensional agents, ensuring that all attributes critical to the simulation are comprehensively represented. To assess the quality of synthetic populations, we compare three generation methods: direct use of original training data, Bayesian Network sampling, and diffusion model. We then evaluate four agent-forecasting approaches: static projection (both idealistic and realistic), resampling, and dynamic projection. While dynamic projection holds potential, it requires complex longitudinal data to model the evolution of agent attributes. To address this, we introduce a heuristic model based on aggregated statistics, though its limitation lies in ignoring attribute correlations, which reduces its accuracy. Our results demonstrate that synthetic populations lose relevance over time, emphasizing the necessity of effective agent-forecasting. Among the methods tested, idealistic static projection yields the best performance but requires data that is difficult to obtain. The other methods show limited improvements, highlighting the ongoing challenges in accurately forecasting agent attributes.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: World Conference on Transport Research, World Conference on Transport Research Society, Jul 2026, Toulouse, France
item.dc:creator: Vianey Darsel (COSYS-GRETTIA), Etienne C{\^o}me (COSYS-GRETTIA), Jeppe Rich (COSYS-GRETTIA), Francisco Camara Pereira (COSYS-GRETTIA), Latifa Oukhellou (COSYS-GRETTIA)

item.title: Numerical and analytical strategies to propagate correlated uncertainties through the discrete Fourier transform
item.description: arXiv:2611.12359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Fourier transform underpins a range of comparisons between atomistic simulations and scattering measurements, yet uncertainty propagation through it is seldom discussed, and correlations between data points are usually ignored. Here, we give a pedagogical account of uncertainty propagation through the discrete Fourier transform, including the full covariance matrix. Two routes are described: a numerical scheme that samples from the multivariate normal distribution describing the data, and an analytical scheme that treats the transform as a change of basis. We discuss the scaling behaviour of these methods and demonstrate their utility on problems that link simulation to scattering: the Faber--Ziman partial structure factors of liquid water, and the dynamic structure factor obtained from a rotational autocorrelation function.
item.dc:creator: Tuguldur Zolzaya, Andrew R. McCluskey

item.title: Bias in Method-of-Moments Heritability Estimation Under Model Misspecification
item.description: arXiv:2611.12615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Method-of-Moments (MoM) based approaches for estimation of variance components --- heritability and beyond --- are central in computational genetics due to their flexibility in addressing diverse and complex models while minimizing assumptions, and ease of computation and approximation in biobank-scale data. MoM are closely related to other important methods in this area like LD-score regression. A fundamental, highly debated question relates to the bias inherent in MoM estimates of variance components when the fitted model is misspecified: since the true underlying model is unknown, the fitted model may be missing some of the components from the true model or contain superfluous ones. We offer a general mathematical formulation of this bias and investigate its properties. This leads to novel insights about the sign and the magnitude of the bias in settings of interest and allows extensions and re-interpretation of previous MoM results in the literature. One case study we pursue is in estimating gene-environment interaction variance components (GxE). We prove that when omitting environment-specific noise components (NxE), the resulting GxE estimates are strictly upward biased, even when no true interaction exists. In another case study, we consider heritability estimation, when the genetic variance components are incorrectly partitioned (such as using a single genome-wide component instead of chromosome-specific components). We derive explicit expressions for the bias in the estimate of genome-wide heritability and its dependence on LD scores within and between components. For example, if all components have the same average LD score, the misspecified heritability estimate is still unbiased.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Gal, Sriram Sankararaman, Saharon Rosset

item.title: Modeling inter-exceedance times of extreme heat days
item.description: arXiv:2611.12633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extreme heat days, here defined as exceedances of a local calendar-day-based 95% quantile, often occur in clusters forming multi-day heatwaves. A calendar-day based threshold allows for the detection of temperature extremes across all seasons, which may impact several economic sectors, public health and ecosystems. Previous approaches to modeling the occurrences of extreme heat events typically treat heat event duration and the time between heat events separately. We propose modeling the inter-exceedance times (IETs) between extreme heat days, allowing for a unified description within a single model. We consider several candidate distributions for the IETs of extreme heat days and find that the zero-inflated discrete Weibull (ZIDW) distribution clearly provides the best fit according to Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests. The ZIDW distribution is a flexible model for count data exhibiting excess zeros as well as over- and under-dispersion: the zero-inflation component captures the pronounced clustering of heat days, while the discrete Weibull component adequately accounts for over-dispersion. Heat days are extracted using both trend-adjusted and non-trend-adjusted thresholds. This allows the analysis of general changes in the occurrence of extreme heat days as well as changes after accounting for the general increase in temperature.
item.dc:creator: Merle Mendel, Roland Fried, Nils Weitzel

item.title: Network Reconstruction via Jeffreys Prior under Missing Sufficient Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2604.05745v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Methods for the reconstruction of economic networks from aggregate information are important for modeling, analysis and policymaking. The traditional Fitness Model (FM) achieves good performance by using node-specific variables that are easily accessible (e.g., GDP for countries or total assets for banks or firms) and the overall link density as the only sufficient statistics. However, it often ignores additional contextual or mesoscopic features which may be more difficult to observe. Here we extend the framework by incorporating block structure as in the Fitness-Corrected Block Model (FCBM), which allows for heterogeneous densities within and across blocks, but in the deliberately more challenging setting where such block-specific densities are not empirically available. Our method uses a Jeffreys prior to provide an unbiased distribution of all compatible solutions and associated entropies, that are otherwise left unidentified, and selects a single reconstruction at the median of this entropy distribution to compensate for the missing sufficient statistics. We evaluate the procedure on nine international-trade networks using GDP as node fitness and World Bank regions as an externally specified partition. The method systematically outperforms the baseline Block-Agnostic FM (which uses the same observed network input statistic) and sometimes even the FCBM (which always uses more information). Controlled synthetic networks confirm that the median is the best of four entropy-based representatives for a range of densities and regional effects similar to the empirical ones, while other representatives can perform better when parameters are pushed far from their realistic range. Overall, our method compensates for missing sufficient statistics via a median-entropy estimate that is empirically very robust within a realistic range of parameters.
item.dc:creator: Minh Duc Duong, Diego Garlaschelli

item.title: Update Slope Is Bounded by Prior Calibration: A Structural Bound and Its Contingent Empirical Signature
item.description: arXiv:2611.10325v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluations of LLM forecasters increasingly measure how forecasts improve as richer evidence is supplied. We identify two confounds in this update-slope metric. First, outcome-aware evidence construction substantially inflates measured responsiveness: on the same models and questions, slopes are roughly four times larger than with resolution-blinded evidence ladders. Second, update slope is a change score with a prior-dependent structural ceiling, so raw comparisons can reflect differences in starting calibration rather than updating behavior. The ceiling defines only a feasible region; whether slope and prior calibration are empirically coupled depends on headroom utilization and varies across our Manifold, ForecastBench, and ACLED pools. Despite this variability, conditioning on prior calibration roughly triples the association between intermediate updating and final Brier score under both blinded and outcome-aware construction. Question identity also explains substantially more variance than model identity across the evaluated pools. We recommend building evidence ladders blind to outcomes, conditioning on prior calibration, and reporting headroom-normalized measures alongside raw slopes.
item.dc:creator: Ben Jenkins, Mihaela Cardei

item.title: A General Statistical Framework for Attention and Manipulation Checks
item.description: arXiv:2611.10515v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attention and manipulation checks are widely used in survey experiments to assess respondents' attentiveness and engagement with treatment, respectively. Yet these checks are subject to measurement error, which may itself depend on treatment when checks are administered after treatment exposure. Restricting analyses to respondents who pass these checks can therefore introduce substantial bias. We propose a general statistical framework for analyzing survey experiments with pre- or post-treatment attention and manipulation checks while accounting for measurement error. We show that three separate checks suffice to identify the proportion of respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment, provided that the checks are conditionally independent among treated respondents given their true, unobserved attentiveness or manipulation status and pre-treatment covariates. Under additional mild assumptions, this result also identifies the average treatment effect among respondents who would be attentive or successfully manipulated under treatment. Building on these identification results, we propose an estimator that allows flexible covariate modeling and establish its asymptotic normality. Applications to framing and digital media literacy experiments demonstrate how accounting for measurement error yields treatment effect estimates that are substantively different from those obtained using conventional approaches.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Nakamura, Kosuke Imai

item.title: How reliable is an embedding of the seabed? Repeat-look measurement of frozen encoders on synthetic aperture sonar
item.description: arXiv:2611.10770v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretrained encoders from self-supervised representation learning are increasingly applied to sonar imagery of the seafloor, where they are evaluated with protocols that take one embedding per target. A target patch of seabed, by contrast, is re-imaged from an alternate look on overlapping survey passes, so each embedding is one measurement of that target. Standard protocols cannot say how consistent those measurements are, or how much of their spread belongs to the patch and how much to the acquisition geometry. We treat this as a measurement-reliability problem. Using a synthetic-aperture sonar (SAS) survey, we measure the repeat-look reliability of embeddings from a frozen natural-image encoder (DINOv3 ViT-S/16). Standard single-look metrics, effective rank, clustering and a linear probe for coral, are all stable to the look, and the probe performs well (AUC 0.93). Yet the repeat-look reliability of the same embeddings is poor, with a distance-based intraclass correlation (dbICC) of 0.20 and nearest neighbours and clusters that barely agree across looks. This contradiction resolves as we find the probe learns a stable direction, whose ICC of 0.60 is 3.0 times that of the full embedding. Variance components, calculated from generalizability theory, attribute under a tenth of the within-cell spread to look acquisition geometry. The rest is cell-specific and cannot be separated without repeat passes at matched geometry. A sonar-pretrained encoder (BenthicDINO) and a classical SAS texture descriptor show the same pattern. For this dataset and the tested representations, uses that depend on patch identity fail, such as cross-pass comparison and retrieval, while uses at the level of habitat type (e.g. coral classification) do not. Because the standard metrics did not detect this, we argue that repeat-look reliability should accompany any evaluation of representations of the seafloor.
item.dc:creator: Harold Horsley, Oscar Pizarro, Hayat Rajani, Morten Omholt Alver

item.title: Gendered Misclassification from Surname-Based Race Imputation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Researchers increasingly estimate political behavior based on race and gender from voter files, where race is imputed from surnames and geography. This only works where surnames suggest group membership, an assumption violated where surnames follow norms around marriage. Imputation is therefore biased against women who adopt their husband's surname, especially those who racially inter-marry, an outcome itself endogenous to partisanship. Using six US states recording self-reported race, I show that imputation is less accurate for Asian and Hispanic women, particularly those sharing the surname of a partner of another race, who differ politically from other women of their race. This violates assumptions behind downstream inference approaches, which nearly double the gender gap in partisanship among Asian voters. I derive an expression showing the bias is largest where a group is small. Using maiden rather than marriage-adopted surnames in North Carolina raises accuracy up to fourfold for women married across racial lines. Recovering maiden surnames, or omitting the married surname, removes much of the bias. In a national replication of a study of gender gaps in turnout, the correction more than triples the gap among Asian voters. In Lebanon, where wives register in their husband's locality, the error enters through geography.
item.dc:creator: Noah Dasanaike

item.title: Combining rock typing and NMR logging to estimate permeability in complex carbonate formations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11150v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating intrinsic permeability from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) logs is difficult in heterogeneous carbonates because a single calibration may not represent distinct pore systems. We evaluated whether flow-zone-indicator (FZI)-based rock typing improves empirical calibration of the modified Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) model in the Arbuckle Group, Kansas. The analysis used 470 depth-matched core-permeability and NMR measurements from the Wellington and Cutter wells. FZI calculated from measured permeability and NMR-derived porosity was grouped using K-means clustering. Six clusters were identified, but one singleton cluster was excluded, leaving five rock types for SDR calibration. Relative to the global model (without clustering), rock-type-specific calibration reduced testing root mean square log-transformed error (RMSLE) from 1.215 to 0.240-0.427 and increased coefficient of determination (CD) from -0.106 to 0.578-0.924. The fitted porosity exponents ranged from 0.053 to 0.521, indicating that porosity provided limited additional information in some rock types and that the SDR parameters should be treated as empirical calibration quantities. Because measured permeability was used to calculate the FZI before the within-cluster splits, these results represent conditional performance for samples with known FZI membership, not blind permeability prediction. Field implementation will require a permeability-independent method for assigning rock types.
item.dc:creator: Nihal Malavalli Lokesh, Biswajit Thander, Esmail Ansari, Ali Eghbali, Behzad Ghanbarian

item.title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
item.description: arXiv:2611.11324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.
item.dc:creator: Chung-I Huang, Wen-Yi Chang

item.title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2611.11483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.
item.dc:creator: Youmi Suk, Yuxuan Li

item.title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions
item.description: arXiv:2611.11493v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.
item.dc:creator: Lydia T. Liu, Kara Schechtman, Pengyi Shi, Angela Zhou

item.title: Can the Remaining Answers Change the Prediction? Worst-Case Stability Checks for Personalized Rating Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.11733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Missing ratings can overturn a personalized model's current prediction. For completed models with additive response scores, exact worst case bounds check all missing assignments without changing the current predictor. We evaluate this audit retrospectively in two self-triage cohorts, 108 clinicians rating three simulated psychiatric interviews, and 126 counseling demonstrations annotated by ten experts. Under shared random half histories, Fisher adaptation based on observed ratings reduces log loss relative to response frequency by 0.1071 nats in the clinician audit (95% CI [0.0867,0.1261]) and 0.0223 in counseling (95% CI[0.0121,0.0321]). The counseling test excludes target experts and source videos from training. Certification covers 5.4% and 10.5% of targets; fixed width acquisition raises coverage to 13.7% and 28.6% at the same budgets. With weights and responses held fixed, the observed-rating update also has lower loss than an affine partial update while certifying exactly the same evaluated targets. The certificate establishes agreement with the completed model, not correctness or stability at intermediate updates. These rating tasks test the method; clinical usefulness remains untested.
item.dc:creator: Priyanka Siddappa, Muntaqim Ahmed Raju, Shifat Haider Al Amin, Ruizhe Ma

item.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
item.description: arXiv:2611.11796v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.
item.dc:creator: Yiqun T. Chen, Jan Matthias, Jianing Yao, Hongyu Eric Zhao, Stephanie C. Hicks

item.title: Severity-Controlled Prediction Sets for Medication Recommendation
item.description: arXiv:2611.11847v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medication recommendation is a multi-label prediction task. However, existing prediction-set evaluation and calibration methods rely mainly on exact-overlap metrics and therefore treat all missed medications as equally severe, overlooking how closely the prediction set matches them within the medication hierarchy. To address this, we introduce Conformal Severity Control (CSC), a post-hoc framework for calibrating medication prediction sets under hierarchy-aware mismatch severity. CSC uses the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) hierarchy to quantify mismatch severity and controls patient-level severity without retraining the predictor, supporting both average severity and upper-quantile severity for the highest-severity mismatches. Experiments on MIMIC-IV show that CSC tracks user-specified severity tolerances and shifts prediction sets away from distant mismatches toward exact or close matches.
item.dc:creator: Yu Gu, Zijun Yu, Chi-Kuang Yeh, Xinyu Wang, Ziyang Song

item.title: A Semiparametric Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Model with a Nonparametric Count Distribution for Seizure Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.11928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Functional count data arise when recurrent events are recorded repeatedly over time and scientific interest centers on how event rates evolve over time and across experimental conditions. Standard mixed effects models for counts have interpretable mean structures but require a parametric conditional distribution, which can be restrictive in the presence of overdispersion, unusual zero frequencies and heavy tails. To address these challenges, we develop the functional count DPGLM (fcDPGLM), a semiparametric Bayesian mixed model that combines GLM-style regression with a nonparametric count distribution. Parametric condition-specific mean trajectories and subject-specific random effects determine the conditional mean exactly, allowing the interpretation of contrasts as usual, while remaining details of the count distribution are learned nonparametrically from the data. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models are recovered as limiting cases. A gamma completely random measure representation allows for efficient posterior simulation. In simulations mimicking a rat seizure study, fcDPGLM estimated mean contrasts as accurately as a correctly specified negative-binomial mixed model, and more accurately otherwise, and recovered zero and exceedance probabilities that the parametric models misrepresent. In the seizure study, seizure rates rise and then decline in the early period after induced status epilepticus but remain high and nearly flat in the chronic period, and rats differ substantially. Poisson and negative-binomial mixed models estimate similar mean trajectories and period contrasts, but only fcDPGLM matches the observed zero frequency, variance and high-burden days.
item.dc:creator: Entejar Alam, Elizabeth Juarez-Colunga, Marco I. Gonz\'alez, Peter M\"uller

item.title: Bayesian precision factor models for high-dimensional macroeconomic time series
item.description: arXiv:2611.12368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Series in a macroeconomic panel are almost all correlated with one another, which makes correlation a poor guide to which pairs are directly linked. For example, Treasury rates at different maturities are all highly correlated, yet a short and a long rate may be related only through the rates at maturities between them; similarly, sectors of the economy such as output, employment, prices, and interest rates may be related directly or only through other series. Both are questions about the inverse covariance matrix. Recovering it from quarterly data is difficult: contemporaneous dependence is entangled with temporal dynamics, the innovations remain densely dependent once those dynamics are removed, and the number of series is comparable to the number of quarters observed. We propose VAPOR (Vector Autoregressive Precision factOR), a Bayesian model that estimates vector autoregressive dynamics jointly with a factor-structured innovation precision matrix, inferring the partial correlations directly from the fitted precision rather than imposing a zero pattern. Applied to 100 quarterly FRED-QD series, VAPOR learns from the data that each Treasury rate is directly related only to the rates at adjacent maturities, places all 26 selected dependencies within a single FRED-QD group, and attains the lowest held-out prediction error among the estimators compared.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dunson

item.title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
item.description: arXiv:2611.12640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Hank Tang (University of Pennsylvania), Peng Yang (The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center), Jiayi Xin (University of Pennsylvania), Tianqi Shang (University of Pennsylvania), Xuyang Chen (University of Pennsylvania), Ying Yuan (The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center), Yi Lian (University of Pennsylvania), Qi Long (University of Pennsylvania)

item.title: Automating structural reliability analysis with a multi-agent large language model framework
item.description: arXiv:2607.16580v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Structural reliability analysis supports the design and safety assessment of buildings and civil infrastructure but requires specialized expertise throughout the workflow. This study presents a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework that automates component-level reliability analysis from a natural-language problem statement to interpreted estimates of the reliability index and failure probability. Specialized agents handle problem formulation, method planning, code generation, execution, and result interpretation, with human confirmation at key decision points. Numerical reliability estimates are not generated by an LLM; instead, they are obtained solely through deterministic execution of validated solvers. This design mitigates the risk of hallucinated numerical outputs and supports reproducibility. The Method Planner is fine-tuned using quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) for a priori reliability-method category selection. The framework uses open-weight models and supports local execution without closed APIs. Results show that it lowers the expertise barrier to structural reliability assessment while preserving computational trustworthiness.
item.dc:creator: Jaehwan Jeon, Chang Hee Lee, Jinhyun Choo, Taeyong Kim

item.title: Evidence on Slowing Progress in Longevity -- Is it Misleading?
item.description: arXiv:2608.07223v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A growing literature argues that progress in human longevity is slowing, and that this slowdown may signal an approaching biological limit to lifespan. The argument rests on visible flattening of cumulative life expectancy records, evaluated through linear regressions or through comparisons of average gains across decades. These summaries, however, provide only weak evidence for slowing improvements, because they cannot distinguish a true from an apparent slowdown. An apparent slowdown may arise due to periods of low variance around unchanged mean annual gains. Applying a Bayesian change-point framework to annual gains, both at the best-practice frontier and separately for each record-holding country, we find no evidence that the expected annual gain has changed across nearly two centuries, but strong evidence that its variance has moved through distinct historical regimes, with progress most regular in recent decades. The recent flattening is consistent with a low-variance regime and provides little evidence for a decline in the underlying mean pace of improvement. Claims that the best-practice frontier signals a biological ceiling should therefore not rest on the recent bend in the cumulative record alone. The frontier is better read as an empirical benchmark, the highest country-specific survival achieved under observed historical conditions.
item.dc:creator: Silvio C. Patricio, Annette Baudisch

item.title: BayesJudge: Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian Meta-Evaluation of Human and LLM Judgments
item.description: arXiv:2610.11116v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI evaluation pipelines often produce conflicting judgments rather than clean labels. Yet existing methods largely collapse disagreement into a single hard label. As a result, item ambiguity, rater biases, and the position preferences of LLM judges are erased together: evaluation outcomes appear deterministic while concealing the underlying uncertainty, and may even systematically favor one response. This conflict is especially acute in pairwise LLM evaluation. We propose \textbf{BayesJudge}, an online Bayesian meta-evaluation layer for conflicting human-LLM judgment streams. BayesJudge treats the latent preference of each item as a latent variable and jointly models two sources of evaluator bias: rater-specific confusion matrices for human annotation bias, and an explicit order parameter for the position preference of LLM judges, thereby separating response quality from evaluator bias. We derive an exact online posterior recursion and adopt a scalable Rao-Blackwellized assumed-density sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) approximation for streaming inference. Consequently, each comparison yields not a single hard label but a posterior distribution over each response winning (as well as a tie or ambiguity state), together with posterior estimates of the bias parameters, making evaluation uncertainty explicit and quantifiable. On synthetic data, BayesJudge accurately recovers human annotation biases and LLM position biases online, and strictly outperforms variants that freeze either bias channel in held-out predictive log-likelihood. On the real-world SummEval dataset, BayesJudge detects systematic order effects in LLM judgments, distinguishes the behavioral signatures of experts and crowdworkers without rater metadata, and yields posterior uncertainty that reflects genuine human disagreement. Our code is available at https://github.com/Killerofthecard/BayesJudge.git
item.dc:creator: Jiahao Zhang, Pengbin Feng, Chunlei Meng, Hang He, Tianyong Hao

item.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy
item.description: arXiv:2611.06376v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. Its remaining life expectancy has no known closed form, and numerical evaluation alone does not reveal how the immaturity hazard enters it. We show that the remaining-lifetime distribution at age $x$ is Gompertz--Makeham with a Poisson-distributed Makeham term. Successive Makeham terms differ by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines, and the Poisson mean is the cumulative immaturity hazard remaining after age $x$. In a latent-clock construction, individuals carry a Poisson number of constant-rate clocks, and selection removes those carrying more clocks first. Integrating the mixture yields an exact series for remaining life expectancy with a closed-form truncation bound. The life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality is close to the probability of carrying a clock times life expectancy with that hazard removed, with a closed-form error bound. In annual fits to Swedish female mortality, this loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, a decline equal to 15\% of the gain in life expectancy at birth, and the approximation was always within 0.06 years.
item.dc:creator: Silvio C. Patricio

item.title: High-Dimensional Markov-Switching Ordinary Differential Processes
item.description: arXiv:2501.00087v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex systems often evolve in continuous time but are observed only at discrete time points with measurement noise. When the interactions can change across unobserved states, recovering both the state transitions and the differential equations is important for mechanistic insight and for identifying time-varying directed graphs. However, this recovery is challenging in high dimensions. In this paper, we study estimation and graph recovery for high-dimensional Markov-switching ordinary differential equation models from noisy discrete observations. We model the switching between states by a latent continuous-time Markov chain, and within each state the drift is a sparse additive function with unknown nonlinear components. We approximate each component by a finite basis expansion and estimate the parameters under group sparsity. Our procedure estimates the latent trajectories by wavelet smoothing and then runs a penalized surrogate expectation-maximization algorithm. Under stationarity and geometric $\beta$-mixing, given a sufficiently accurate estimated trajectory and other local regularity conditions, we show that the algorithm converges geometrically to a neighborhood of the true parameters. Finally, in an application to resting-state fMRI data, the procedure identifies multiple connectivity states, whose occupation times we compare descriptively between the children with combined-type ADHD and the typically developing children used in the fit.
item.dc:creator: Katherine Tsai, Mladen Kolar, Sanmi Koyejo

item.title: Online Multivariate Regularized Distributional Regression for High-dimensional Probabilistic Electricity Price Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2504.02518v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probabilistic electricity price forecasting (PEPF) is vital for short-term electricity markets, yet the multivariate nature of day-ahead prices - spanning 24 consecutive hours - remains underexplored. At the same time, real-time decision-making requires methods that are both accurate and fast. We introduce an online algorithm for multivariate distributional regression models, allowing efficient modeling of the conditional means, variances, and dependence structures of electricity prices. The approach combines multivariate distributional regression with online coordinate descent and LASSO-type regularization (absolute shrinkage and selection operator), enabling scalable estimation in high-dimensional covariate spaces. Additionally, we propose a regularized estimation path over increasingly complex dependence structures, allowing for early stopping and avoiding overfitting. In a case study using historical data from the German day-ahead market, the proposed method yields interpretable and well-calibrated joint prediction intervals for the 24-dimensional price distribution and provides robust performance across a range of proper scoring rules. The results underscore the importance of modeling the dependence structure of electricity prices. Furthermore, we analyze the trade-off between predictive accuracy and computational costs for batch and online estimation and provide a high-performing open-source Python implementation in the ondil package.
item.dc:creator: Simon Hirsch

item.title: Comparative e-backtesting
item.description: arXiv:2511.05840v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Backtesting risk measures is a central task in financial regulation. While traditional backtests evaluate whether a forecasting model is statistically consistent with observed losses, regulatory practice often requires assessing the performance of an internal model relative to standard models. In this paper, we develop a parametric anytime-valid framework for comparative backtests of general risk measures using e-values and e-processes. We construct likelihood-based e-processes for comparative e-backtests with validity and power guarantees. As practical guidelines, we propose the e-three-zone approach based on weak dominance, and introduce the overall and resetting test schemes for different practical purposes. Simulation studies and empirical analyses are conducted to show practical manipulations in financial regulation.
item.dc:creator: Zhanyi Jiao, Qiuqi Wang, Yimiao Zhao

item.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2602.00387v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay. By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is \emph{singular} with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field's independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.
item.dc:creator: Mame Diarra Toure, David A. Stephens

item.title: Towards Reliable LLM Evaluation: Correcting the Winner's Curse in Adaptive Benchmarking
item.description: arXiv:2605.05973v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adaptive prompt and program search makes LLM evaluation selection-sensitive. Once benchmark items are reused inside tuning, the observed winner's score need not estimate the fresh-data performance of the full tune-then-deploy procedure. We study inference for this procedure-level target under explicit tuning budgets. We propose SIREN, a selection-aware repeated-split reporting protocol that freezes the post-search shortlist, separates splitwise selection from held-out evaluation, and uses an item-level Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for uncertainty quantification. In a fixed-shortlist regime with smooth stabilized selection, the estimator admits a first-order item-level representation, and the bootstrap yields valid simultaneous inference on a finite budget grid. This supports confidence intervals for procedure-performance curves and pre-specified equal-budget and cross-budget comparisons. Controlled simulations and MMLU-Pro tuning experiments show that winner-based reporting can be optimistic and can change deployment conclusions, while SIREN remains close to the finite-sample reporting target.
item.dc:creator: Jiefu Zhang, Yang Xu, Haixiang Sun, Zihan Zhou, Tianyu Cao, Vaneet Aggarwal

item.title: Separate versus Pooled Winsorization in Difference-in-Differences: Bias, Efficiency, and Finite-Sample Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2606.15097v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: \textit{\textbf{Problem Definition: }} Extreme outcomes are common in operational data, and empirical difference-in-differences (DiD) studies often winsorize them to limit their influence. Yet winsorization can change both the estimated treatment effect and its sampling uncertainty. We ask when winsorization improves DiD estimation and whether cutoffs should be computed separately within each group-period cell or from observations pooled across cells. \textit{\textbf{Methodology/Results: }} We develop finite-sample and asymptotic analyses in a two-group, two-period DiD setting. For continuous outcomes with finite variance, separate winsorization achieves a uniform sub-Gaussian deviation guarantee under a calibrated winsorization fraction, while neither raw DiD nor pooled winsorization can achieve the same guarantee. We identify conditions under which separate winsorization is asymptotically unbiased, whereas pooled winsorization with a fixed fraction may remain biased. Under these conditions, standard tail classifications alone do not establish an efficiency ranking. Yet a two-sided decreasing-failure-rate (DFR) condition on each cell's error distribution can guarantee strictly smaller asymptotic variance for separate winsorization than for raw DiD at every fixed winsorization fraction. Numerical results support both analyses. \textit{\textbf{Managerial Implications: }} Our results guide practitioners on whether and how to winsorize outcomes in DiD studies, clarifying the advantages and limitations of raw DiD, separate winsorization, and pooled winsorization. The DFR condition arising from our efficiency analysis offers a simple diagnostic for when winsorization can be expected to lower asymptotic variance while keeping the treatment-effect estimate unbiased, giving theoretical grounding to a practice that has so far rested mainly on convention.
item.dc:creator: Chao Cheng (Washington University in St. Louis), Chenshan Hu (University of Colorado Boulder), Yukai Huang (Suffolk University)

item.title: Choosing the Dictionary and Penalty for IV-LASSO
item.description: arXiv:2609.07033v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Estimating an instrumental variables (IV) first stage with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) requires choosing a dictionary and penalty. Existing rules target first-stage objectives rather than precision of the structural parameter estimate. We derive a feasible approximate mean squared error (AMSE) criterion for full-sample IV-LASSO with one endogenous regressor and homoskedastic Gaussian errors. For a prespecified list of dictionary-penalty pairs, the criterion trades off approximation of the optimal instrument against a complexity cost that depends on the first two moments of the LASSO effective dimension and on the degree of endogeneity. The selected pair attains the smallest candidate-specific AMSE component up to vanishing relative error. In simulations calibrated to Paravisini et al. (2015), the criterion improves substantially on plug-in rules at low endogeneity and on cross-validation at high endogeneity, with nearly identical results under non-Gaussian errors. A supplementary appendix formally extends analysis to a class of non-Gaussian errors.
item.dc:creator: Yukun Ma, Manu Navjeevan, Bogdan Salahub

item.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.08443v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, adaptive group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.
item.dc:creator: Rohan Hemant Chhatre, Chiranjit Dutta, Nalini Ravishanker, Sumanta Basu

item.title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14695v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.
item.dc:creator: Michael B\"ucker

item.title: Balanced State Subspaces with Spectral Rank Allocation for Mamba-2 State Compression
item.description: arXiv:2610.36617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune coordinates with per-channel scores. Trained states are nearly rank-one and bias-like, aligned with the mean write; but the output's energy spans an order of magnitude more directions. Per-channel scores see only the diagonal of the write--read operator, so they cannot select the subspace that governs the input--output map, which is a rotation of the coordinates. We therefore propose \method{}, which keeps that subspace by applying balanced truncation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Layers differ just as sharply: most are bias-dominated, while the few that carry long-range associations are the flattest and need most of their state. We therefore introduce \spar{}, which redistributes a fixed total rank budget across layers according to the Hankel spectrum. On Mamba-2 checkpoints from 130M to 2.7B, \method{}+\spar{} halves the state at an average cost of $0.3$ WikiText-2 perplexity points, against $1.6$ for GHOST, while retaining $97\%$ of the dense model's five-digit in-context recall. At a quarter of the state, giving every layer the same rank keeps $5\%$ of that recall and \spar{} $77\%$, for a $7\%$ perplexity cost.
item.dc:creator: Shang Tingyu, Cao Wenfei, Han Zhi
